Treat technical translation as target-user usability work, not as source-text transfer alone.
Equip technical translators with technical communication, usability, subject, research, genre, and writing competence.
Train technical translators in technical communication and treat technical translation as information design and engineering.

Be a good technical writer in order to be a good technical translator — their principal stylistic goals coincide — and adopt technical writers' writing strategies and audience-analysis methods, while accepting that information design, typography, and layout are usually beyond the translator's remit.
Shape translated documentation around reader cognition, including perception, memory, attention, learning, and problem solving.
Match target-language technical conventions and required document form while preserving correctness and usability.
Build or infer a robust translation brief covering intended use, audience, publication status, terminology, style constraints, legal constraints, and document conventions.

Base translation decisions on who will read the text, how they will use it, and how it will be distributed, and establish these via a translation brief specifying at minimum the target audience, the intended purpose (information vs publication), and any stylistic or terminological requirements.
Distinguish technical translation from adjacent specialized domains before choosing strategy or evaluating success.
Choose technical-translation strategy from the communicative situation and project criteria rather than universal maxims.
Use source-external resources and technical-writing interventions whenever the source text alone is insufficient for target-user function.
Let target-user needs govern additions, omissions, condensation, restructuring, and explicitness.
Provide enough information for the current user purpose, avoiding both overload and under-specification.
Make safety-critical information explicit, repeated where needed, and escalated to the client when the source is deficient.
Balance fidelity, intelligibility, speed, cost, audience need, and target-culture acceptability instead of pursuing abstract perfection.
Handle culture-specific references according to the target user need for precision, explanation, or local usability.
Define target-text function pragmatically from purpose, audience, initiator, translator, and situation; do not infer it from the source text alone.
Minimize target-reader processing effort by making context, intended interpretation, and given-new progression easy to follow.
Use reader evidence, usability studies, and style guidance to judge what the target audience will accept as good technical documentation.
Subject user documentation to legal, standards, accuracy, completeness, safety, readability, layout, and hands-on usability quality assurance.
Make target-relevant information easy to find, select, assimilate, and proportionally redundant.
Apply function plus loyalty: meet target-reader expectations while respecting source-side intentions and stakeholder relationships.
Combine literal translation, paraphrase, modification, addition, omission, and other strategies locally under one communicative purpose.
Concentrate strategy decisions on target audience needs and native-quality technical communication.
Plan documentation around specific readers, their tasks, prior knowledge, problems, and objectives.
Treat technical documentation as collaborative designed communication whose tools, formats, roles, and purposes affect translation work.

Treat scientific and technical translation as a communicative service for people and produce a target text that functions as an authentic target-language document, because users care most about accessing its information effectively.
Classify document type by communicative purpose before deciding content, structure, and rhetorical strategy.
Make user guides task-centered teaching interfaces rather than repositories of system information.
Protect reader safety and prevent product damage before pursuing other instructional goals.
Use summaries, glossaries, indices, and informative tables of contents to improve access and retrieval.
Preserve user trust by making guides correct, confidence-building, and clearly oriented to customer needs.
Design user guides to support starting, productivity, troubleshooting, and experience-level differences.
Account for international readers through audience-specific linguistic and cultural adaptation.
Treat appearance, layout, typography, white space, and format as communicative usability factors, not decoration.
Choose delivery medium according to how users actually read and use the documentation.
Use graphics deliberately and control translated screenshots against the final localized interface.
Choose user-guide structure from product nature, audience background, and user tasks while avoiding information overload.
Build modular, navigable guides with small functional task units, meaningful headings, useful overviews, and reader progress points.
Adapt headings and information structure in translation to target-reader expectations.
Be honest, comprehensive enough, accurate, and ethically adequate at the point of need.
Write concise, direct, audience-fit user-guide language without ambiguity, obscuring euphemism, unnecessary jargon, or unexplained acronyms.
Use repetition, sentence flow, and parallel structure only when they reinforce action, memory, clarity, or habit formation.
Evaluate user guides holistically with representative task-based usability testing; readability formulas are only partial indicators.
Treat the user guide as part of overall system usability and judge guide quality holistically.
Evaluate usability for specified users, goals, and contexts through effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
Design visual presentation around human perception: balance contrast, limit color codes, avoid all-cap running text, and use Gestalt grouping deliberately.
Reduce working-memory burden through chunking, short retention gaps, familiar groupings, relevant visuals, and recognition-based cues.
Minimize attention switching because reading the guide and doing the task draw on the same limited cognitive capacity.
Prime and teach new material by linking it to related concepts, existing schemes, examples, habits, and visible reinforcement.
Use repetition and practice to support procedural automaticity without creating unnecessary dependence.
Help users frame problems correctly, surface misconceptions, and provide enough declarative background before expecting fluent action.
Serve multiple proficiency levels with predictable novice support and efficient reference for experienced users.
Build usability from the start using cognetics, explicit goals, and measurable criteria.
Judge efficiency from the user total task, and keep guide information clear, digestible, and concise.
Prevent likely errors, make recovery easy, and use consistent familiar terminology and interaction patterns.
Support both reading-to-learn and reading-to-do, including sequential reading and random lookup.
Implement usability through a hierarchy of principles, guidelines, local rules, and style guides, while still validating with users.
Apply iconic linkage by expressing recurring semantically identical information with the same target-language construction and preserving latent repetition.
Use one-idea sentences and uniform phrasing to reduce memory load, build habits, improve recognition, and free attention for the task.
Accept reduced stylistic variation in technical instructions when consistency increases clarity and reduces ambiguity.
Establish usability with evaluation rather than design confidence alone.
Select evaluation methods from the test question and required data, distinguishing formative, summative, analytical, empirical, absolute, and comparative methods.
Prefer indirect overt recording when observer effects would distort performance, while preserving ethical recording practice.
Avoid think-aloud protocols when representative task performance is the measurement target.
Combine objective observation with carefully designed subjective instruments.
Recruit representative participants, balance relevant skills across comparative groups, and use small-sample statistics appropriate to usability studies.
Define a small, observable, product-relevant set of performance criteria before testing.
Prefer post-task or private ratings over concurrent public questioning when task integrity and candidness matter.
Prepare users and materials so participants critique the product and guide, not themselves, without being distracted by avoidable text errors.
Build guide quality early and improve it iteratively with user involvement and pilot studies.
In comparative documentation studies, isolate the manipulated variable and keep fonts, layout, graphics, content, and other confounds equivalent.
Introduce iconic linkage with test materials that contain suitably spaced recurrence, a concise style guide, and translation-memory support.
Choose test software and tasks that make participants rely on the guide rather than prior product knowledge.
Protect participants through informed consent, anonymized identifiers, confidentiality, and a comfortable realistic test environment.
Measure satisfaction and retention with instruments that fit the study cost, realism, and time constraints.
Measure retention, task time, error rates, and satisfaction with explicit instruments and report the aggregate outcomes.
Capture screen interaction when understanding performance requires seeing what happens in the software.
Use screen logging or recording suited to the application interaction style instead of over-shoulder observation.
Ensure comparative groups have enough participants and protect sessions from cross-participant contamination.
Familiarize participants with context, acclimate them to recording, and capture useful informal comments without letting them drive scoring.
Drop, redefine, or redesign metrics and tasks that cannot be observed reliably or that are confounded by participant traits or prior knowledge.
Script administrator instructions and question handling to prevent session-to-session variability.
Use the pilot to correct tasks, tools, methods, criteria, and materials before running the main study.
Run main studies with realistic users and settings while preserving comparability with the pilot and handling venue constraints.
Treat administrator help as a guide-failure signal by directing users to the guide first and counting each escalation.
Analyze very small usability comparisons with exact nonparametric tests, aggregate measures, and exclusion of fixed-duration tasks from timing.
Match participants to the real work context and domain when task performance depends on contextual knowledge.
Triangulate subjective ratings with objective performance and recall measures.
Treat the main study as empirical support that iconic linkage can improve speed, errors, completion, recall, satisfaction, clarity, and learning.
Use unchanged layout/content controls and multi-metric improvements to rule out likely confounds.
Do not assume consistency is disruptive; inconsistent instruction phrasing may be more harmful than repeated structures.
Account for prior-tool interference when designing tasks and guides.
Evaluate documentation strategies through summative user testing that collects both performance and satisfaction data and is refined by pilot work.
Ground technical translation in target-audience communicative service, Skopos purpose, and reader cognitive demands.
Use iconic linkage only where recurring information makes standardisation practical, and treat it as one cognitive strategy among others.
Scale consistency through controlled language, style guides, translation memory, and improved semantic-match tooling.
Preserve usability-study instruments and participant-level tables so study procedures and results can be audited.
Screen and consent participants with role-specific profiles, data-collection disclosure, confidentiality, and clear session tracking.

Distinguish scientific from technical texts by their aim — a technical text exists to convey information as clearly and effectively as possible, while a scientific text analyzes, synthesizes, theorizes, and persuades — because the differing aim drives different language and a different translation strategy.

Recognize that scientific and technical source material spans three overlapping information categories — results of pure science, results of applied research on a specific problem, and technologists' work yielding a sellable product — which rest on largely the same underlying knowledge.

Treat scientific and technical terminology as potentially metaphorical and culture-bound, and recognize and negotiate such metaphors much as a literary translator would, because style, metaphor, and creativity are intrinsic to scientific discourse.

Expect scientific texts to use a broader range of linguistic devices (longer, more complex sentences, figurative language) because they aim to create an effect, and treat metaphors as a valuable tool in both scientific and technical texts for naming abstractions and explaining processes through readers' existing knowledge.

For products sold in the EU, ensure all technical documentation is translated into the country-of-sale language(s), treat the translated documentation as an original target-language document subject to target-language technical-writing regulations, and give clear, comprehensible instructions with explicit risk warnings — most stringently for regulated classes (general product safety, toys, medical devices, cosmetics).
Be aware that a translator can be held legally liable for mistakes in a translation, through contractual obligations or tort-law liability.

Do not expect any single translation theory to fully fit scientific and technical translation, and do not force a project into one pole of a binary model (formal vs dynamic, semantic vs communicative, covert vs overt) — real translation involves shades of grey.

Know the equivalence toolkit: formal equivalence matches source form and content; dynamic equivalence matches the source's effect on its audience; and Koller's five levels are denotational, connotational, textual-norm, pragmatic, and linguistic-form equivalence.

Choose which level of equivalence to prioritize by text type — denotational meaning for an instruction manual, linguistic form for a popular-science article, textual norms for a certificate of conformity — accepting lower equivalence on the other levels, and use equivalence levels as translation-time tools rather than post-hoc rules that dictate how the text must be produced.

Treat formal and dynamic equivalence as vague, subjective concepts that rarely yield concrete, actionable guidance on their own, since eliciting the same response from two audiences is inherently uncertain.

Judge and produce a scientific or technical translation by the norms, expectations, and rules of the target language — a translation is a fact of the target language that hosts it (Toury), read as if originally written in the target language.

Let the purpose of the target text (its Skopos), as specified by commissioner and translator, govern the translation rather than the source text; a source is an offer of information from which many valid translations follow once the intended purpose is known.
When a client provides no meaningful brief, construct a working one by asking a few probing questions (such as whether the text is for publication) before translating.

Accept that the translation brief has no settled form and often forces educated guesses, so ask the client a short standard set of questions — kept small so as not to seem unprofessional, since the translator is usually the expert — covering at minimum the target language variety, the purpose (information vs publication), the deadline, and any required terminology.
Check the customer's website to capture the look and feel of their own documents, even when they state no specific language requirements, so the translation reads like one of the client's documents.

Build a practical working method by combining Skopos theory (what the translation must achieve), knowledge of text typologies (what the target text should look like against comparable target texts), and equivalence levels used as translation-time guidelines.

Adapt register and emphasis to the target audience: shift a source register that would misfire (e.g. a patronizing expert-to-layperson tone) and tailor information density versus explanation to the intended reader, since the same source text can legitimately yield different translations for different audiences.

Be able to recognize the specialized file types and software of the client's industry and be comfortable (not necessarily expert) with markup and scripting such as HTML and XML, so you can identify and translate the text without damaging the technical parts of the file — basic word processing alone is no longer enough in sci-tech domains.

Apply CAT tools where they fit: translation memory helps only with high-repetition or frequently-updated (chiefly technical) texts, terminology management helps where a large volume of terms must stay consistent, and TM filters reduce the need to master multiple DTP applications; familiarity with these tools often decides whether a project is awarded.

Expect duties beyond translating — editing, proofreading, and revising other translators' work — and on large team projects rely on an editor or senior translator to combine sections and enforce consistency of style and terminology.
When a client needs to decide whether to commission a full translation, provide a gist (indicative) translation that conveys the basic meaning without stylistic polish.

Determine first what type of translation the client wants, because it drives what is translated, how, and how long it takes: a selective translation renders only certain sections; a gist translation is a rough summary needing less care over style; an information-purposes translation must convey all the information but tolerates rough style for internal use; and a publication-purposes translation demands the best content and flawless language, often with a second reviewer.

Acting as a cultural expert, advise the client whenever a website, advertisement, brand, or company name contains images, colours, language, or content likely to be problematic or cause offence in the target culture.

Frame sci-tech translation as part of technical communication — creating, designing, and transmitting technical information so people can understand it easily and use it safely, effectively, and efficiently (Markel) — and treat the target audience as the single most important variable.

Treat every technical document as a task-oriented tool addressed to a specific audience for a specific purpose — a means to an end, not entertainment or a showcase for the writer — whose goal is to convey the right information to the right people in the right format; where a text serves several readerships, prioritize them and cater accordingly.

Recognize scientific and popular-science texts as an exception to the plain-tool rule: they may legitimately need invented terms, rhetorical devices, and literary creativity to explain, persuade, and entertain.

Expect collaboratively produced documents to carry stylistic and terminological inconsistencies (a concept named differently across the text, uneven clarity), and resolve them — via an editor on team translations — rather than reproducing them.

Respect that design (font, size, colour, white space, graphics) drives usability and that clear prose alone does not guarantee comprehension; a translator can improve usability even without altering layout, changing graphics only when they carry cultural connotations.

Abandon the assumption that only technically knowledgeable people read technical texts — interest or necessity has replaced background knowledge as the key audience assumption, so there is no reliable 'no lay reader' rule.

Categorize readers by role (Horton's novice, occasional, transfer, expert, rote; Markel's experts, technicians, managers, general) to reveal how they use a text — experts skim, novices read in sequence, rote users jump to steps — which for the translator means consistent headings for navigation and short, simple sentences for instructions; treat these categories as useful but oversimplified.

Make the audience the primary driver of translation: nearly every decision (term choice, rewording for clarity or tone, resequencing) depends on understanding it, and in translation the audience factors double because two languages and cultures are involved — so identify the source-text and target-text audiences, reconcile any incompatibility, and, when no brief is given, deduce the likely audience from context and text type.

Ask what the audience already knows about the technology, and let the answer decide whether to add explanations, which facts to foreground or omit, and whether specialized terms and acronyms can be used or must be avoided.

Identify the audience's specific language variety or locale (e.g. US English, Swiss German, Canadian French) rather than just the language, because a language bundles culture, customs, norms, and conventions that shape the text.

Calibrate language and detail to the audience's education, literacy, work experience, expertise, and seniority: overly complex language hurts less-literate readers while pitching too low frustrates literate ones, and the audience's expertise sets how much detail to present and how.

Avoid over-catering a single document to too many audiences; where a text genuinely serves multiple readerships, split them into primary and secondary audiences and label or structure sections so each group's needs are met separately.

For non-native or limited-language readers, limit vocabulary, define new or specialized terms and abbreviations at first use, use the active voice, and avoid long sentences — plain-language strategies that also benefit every reader.

Handle regional language variety and product/drug naming deliberately: not all terminology or cultural references are universally standardized, and the same product is often marketed under different names by market, so swap product or drug names for generic or country-specific equivalents when needed.

Analyze the target culture as more than nationality: cultural norms shape slang and jargon, forms of address, shared-knowledge references, and conventions for date, time, currency, and legal or institutional references; do not equate one culture with one language, and treat cross-cultural models (Hall, Hofstede, Hoft, Trompenaars) as rules of thumb rather than licence to stereotype.

Compare the source and target audiences across educational systems, literacy, learning style, and political, religious, and social climate, as well as their approaches to context, authority, and uncertainty.

Set the level of explicit detail by the audience's high- or low-context orientation (Hall): a text written for a low-context culture can seem patronizing to a high-context audience, and a text for a high-context culture can seem sketchy or confusing to a low-context audience.
Let a culture's attitude to authority (Hofstede's power distance) shape how you address readers, issue instructions, and decide what information to foreground.

Match the amount of explanation to the audience's uncertainty avoidance: high-uncertainty-avoidance readers need explicit detail because they treat the unknown as threatening, while low-uncertainty-avoidance readers work things out and tolerate gaps.
Use a standardized, repeatable, customizable audience-profiling checklist or worksheet to analyze and compare the source and target audiences for a project.

Never accept a translation project without first seeing the text and reading through it, because a text can unexpectedly require unfamiliar specialisms and overstretching risks failing to finish or producing substandard work.

Do not take on a subject whose most basic aspects you do not understand, but do embrace texts that require some research; the ability to research a topic quickly, find the key information, and assimilate it is a translator's most valuable asset.

Identify what kind of text you are dealing with before translating it — the 'writing situation' is the combination of audience and purpose (Markel) — because identifiable basic characteristics indicate the type even when a text cannot be cleanly classified as purely technical or scientific.

Keep language clear, simple, and to the point as a core value of technical communication: use simple declarative sentences rather than complex ones and give instructions in chronological or logical cause-and-effect order, especially for readers who are hurried, stressed, or non-native.

Handle terminology carefully even though it is only about 5-10% of a technical text: abbreviations and acronyms can mean different things by subject, context, or producing organization, and ordinary-looking general words often carry specific technical meanings that must not be translated as everyday vocabulary.

Expect information conveyed as bare facts and specifications (bullet lists or tables in technical texts, sentences in scientific ones) and as cross-references to laws, standards, books, or interface items that avoid overloading the reader and can also signal that a product is reliable and safe by conforming to a standard.

Where a document contains screenshots, treat it as bound to the external software interface: accurately reproduce the text shown in the interface, phrase all references to the software consistently, and update the document whenever the software changes, since a picture of the screen is far more effective than verbal description.

Handle formulae, scientific notation, and units precisely: numbers quantify a physical quantity via units governed largely by SI (seven base units modifiable by prefixes such as micro-, milli-, nano-), and although metric is the international norm, Imperial units still appear in some languages and text types, so always identify the unit system in use.

Preserve equation symbol definitions intact: formulae are compact, accurate, and near-universally intelligible precisely because each symbol is identified, defined, and assigned a value, so the translator must keep those symbol definitions.

Group most scientific and technical texts into recurring types (manuals, applications and proposals, reports and scientific papers, presentations, regulatory documents, popular science) and treat a website as a distribution medium rather than a text type of its own.

For procedural (cookbook-style) manuals use a prerequisites list plus numbered steps and control the information flow so the reader is not overloaded; never combine multiple tasks in a single sentence — split a crammed source sentence into separate ordered steps so the reader immediately knows what to do and in what order.

Make tutorials gentle, supportive, and never confusing, too-advanced, or wrong — because readers tend to blame themselves for problems following instructions even when the text is substandard — keeping information density low and always including the hazard warnings EU law requires; for transfer users, avoid explaining every concept yet do not over-simplify to the point of patronizing them.

In guides — advanced material for readers who already have a basic understanding — adapt the plentiful examples to the target-language culture while retaining the detailed descriptions, figures, tables, and diagrams.

Treat user guides as structured instructional documents in simple language supported by graphics whose usability rests on broadly universal human cognition but also carries culture-specific features and rarely targets a single culture, so translating them is not always straightforward.

When a single document combines a tutorial and a guide, expect its function to shift from instructional to explanatory after the first chapters and change your translation strategy accordingly partway through.

For reference manuals and any cross-referenced document, treat topics as independent, dipped-into units (repeating information where needed to spare readers from skipping back and forth), and keep the names of referenced topics, sections, or documents accurate and consistent — liaising with any other translator handling a referenced section, since a translation memory only auto-suggests wording you translated yourself.
Expect automatically generated reference manuals compiled from programmers' notes and code comments to contain uneven, poor writing, because programmers are not trained writers.
For online help, keep task-based topics discrete, independent, and readable quickly on a single screen with short, simple sentences, because the user's point of entry is unpredictable.

For heterogeneous or hybrid documents whose sections differ in function and style (proposals, tenders, reports, case studies, marketing material), recognize each section's change in function and apply a single document-level macrostrategy supported by local, per-section microstrategies rather than one uniform strategy.

Expect scientific papers and reports to follow a small number of standard structures — chiefly IMRAD (Introduction, Materials and methods, Results, Discussion) or the fuller Abstract, Introduction, Materials, Procedure, Results, Conclusions, References.

Translate an abstract, together with its title, as a self-contained text — it is published separately in abstracting services and readers judge from it whether to read the whole paper — so never leave anything awkward or unclear in an abstract on the assumption it will become clear later.
Expect abstracts written by non-native-speaker authors to be fraught with language errors, and handle those errors rather than reproduce them blindly.

Translate scientific-paper sections to their conventions: keep correct spelling and orthography in the Materials section (proprietary and trademarked names); demand absolute consistency and clarity in the Procedure section, since errors threaten the repeatability of the experiment and the reliability of the study, watching abbreviations, acronyms, units, and ellipsis; and in the Results section translate reported speech exactly as written even if it is not grammatically perfect.

Leave a journal's stipulated bibliographic style (Harvard, MLA, APA) unchanged, but when translating between different scripts decide, or ask the client, whether to transliterate author names and titles, using an ISBN to find any official gloss or transcription.

Treat a case study as a marketing text with a standard structure (identify the client, its needs as the 'problem', the solution and its implementation, a testimonial, and closing company details) that is demanding to translate because it mixes complex technical data with opinion, reported speech, and persuasion, and its language must stay positive without overstating or misrepresenting the product.

Treat a technical case study as a promotional text combining technical, marketing, and journalistic language, with a standard headline/testimonial/problem/solution structure, whose language must reflect a positive client experience without overstating or misrepresenting the product.

For presentations, resolve the inherent ambiguity of bullet-point slides by requesting the speaker's notes or the full paper, and watch translation length: because text boxes do not resize, a longer translation shrinks the font or overflows the slide, so do not add a slide without first checking the client on slide-count, timing, and design limits.

Treat regulatory and normative documents (directives, laws, and standards from bodies such as ISO, DIN, BSI) as unambiguous specification rule-sets with a legal dimension — carrying legal terminology, and, for patents, protecting the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing — and translate them with meticulous factual accuracy and compliance with their specific linguistic requirements.

For medicine product information, conform exactly to the European Medicines Agency's EMEA templates for format, layout, headings, spellings, and established phrases — because deficient product information can get the medicine withdrawn — and reuse the multilingual templates as a ready-made, approved terminology resource.

In popular science, note that much of the source's cautious hedging is often stripped away to simplify, and that the text is hybrid — scientific terminology combined with literary or journalistic devices — which makes it particularly demanding to translate.

Understand why a text is structured as it is — function, circumstances of use, logical progression, and cultural norms — and distinguish linked, cohesive texts from discrete-section texts; in discrete-section texts read in unpredictable order, avoid anaphoric and cataphoric cross-references, instead making a reference specific (naming the chapter) or repeating the necessary information.

Recognize a text's type and genre conventions as a prerequisite to translating it (Bell, Schaffner): genres are socially embedded, some highly culture-specific and some universal, and even ostensibly universal conventions require different micro-level strategies per language (for example, giving instructions with imperatives in English but infinitives in German).
Translate titles and headings to conform with target-culture convention (Nord's title functions), which may mean converting an expressive source title into a purely informative one.

Use Gopferich's function categories (juridical-normative, actualizing, didactic-instructive, compilation) to understand what a text aims to achieve, and give the didactic-instructive category — with its highly heterogeneous audience and greatest number of problems — the most careful audience analysis.

Treat a scientific paper as a written report of original research whose purpose is to both inform and persuade peers of the validity of its observations and conclusions and the effectiveness of its methods.

Expect the precise challenges of a translation to vary with the nature of the text and especially with the language combination and direction — what poses a problem in one target language may pose none in another.

Create a document profile — identifying subject, audience, text function, key features, and potential problems along with strategies for them — as a method for preparing to translate a given text type effectively.

Know the profiles of common technical text types: a technical data sheet covers a product's composition, properties, and applications plus safety, legal, and environmental information; test instructions are standard operating procedures of step-by-step inspection; and expert technical reports (associated with engineering) give the object of study, the test circumstances, and the materials and methods, often produced by an independent specialist.

Treat popular science as a bridge to a general public that sometimes simplifies concepts or states as fact what the underlying science states tentatively, so be aware the source may overstate certainty relative to the science.

Recognize a Certificate of Conformity as a manufacturer's declaration that a product meets European regulations (to ensure free movement of goods), whose product, producer, type-approval, and specification content is defined by EU regulation but varies by product.

Use Vinay and Darbelnet's direct strategies knowingly: direct translation (literal translation, borrowing, calquing) requires less intervention and less deviation from the source, while oblique translation is reserved for when the grammatical, pragmatic, and lexical differences between source and target are too great for a direct approach.

Understand that literal translation is more sophisticated than word-for-word replacement — shifting from word to group to clause once the target stops complying with target-language grammar, and avoiding additions, omissions, and paraphrasing — and is in fact one of the most frequently used strategies in technical texts.
Favour paraphrasing as perhaps the most useful procedure for technical translation, because it avoids interference and unidiomatic constructions caused by sticking too closely to the source text.

Never assume a literal translation is appropriate merely because it is grammatically, syntactically, and idiomatically correct: it can still fail in the target text, because different audiences have expectations about how information is presented to them.

Use borrowing — transferring a source lexical item into the target unmodified except for transliteration — when the target language has no existing word or concept, or deliberately to create a foreign or exotic effect such as evoking the source culture in popular science.

Approach calquing with caution: building a target neologism from the parts of a source word can sound alien and confound readers, so do not coin new words without good reason where acceptable target-language alternatives already exist.

Know the four oblique procedures and when each applies: equivalence replaces source elements with completely different wording that replicates the situation (for idioms, fixed phrases, and warning signs and labels); transposition changes a word's class without changing meaning (nominalization to verb, passive to active or imperative); and modulation shifts the point of view (positive to negative, abstract to concrete, part for whole).

Reserve adaptation as a last resort for a source situation or concept absent from the target culture, and apply its procedures in order: cultural substitution first, then descriptive paraphrase, and only then omission — omitting only as a fully justifiable last resort, since technical documentation is concerned first and foremost with information.

Use expansion — making implicit source content explicit by adding explanatory phrases or connectors — to make the target clearer, improve flow, or compensate for a weaker target-audience background, as when the source was written by an untrained writer, the target audience is less expert, or a high-context source is read by a low-context audience; the resulting semantic redundancy is well tolerated by technical texts.

Use contraction — removing unnecessary, irrelevant, or confusing detail — to fit the target audience's background, driven by their expectations, recognizing that adding or omitting detail risks either patronizing one audience or forcing another to guess.
Clarify a text by recycling information already provided elsewhere in it, expanding the translation with that internal information.

Apply generalizing and particularizing deliberately: generalize (replace a specific term with a generic one) only when the specific term is not essential and can be inferred or relocated, otherwise keep it; and particularize (use a more specific term) when the source term is too broad, ambiguous, or wrongly connoted — which requires understanding the subject well enough to pick the right term, consulting the author, client, or a subject-matter expert.

Ensure a target term carries the same connotations and denotational meaning as the source unless there is a valid reason otherwise, because over- and under-translation can be deliberate strategies but also accidental and harmful — narrowing 'fuel' to 'petrol' in a safety directive created a wrong meaning with safety, financial, and legal consequences.

Use compensation to offset the loss of source-text features by adding features elsewhere in the target text — to balance the information load or make the style more consistent — in the four forms: compensation in kind, in place, by splitting, and by merging.

Respect that technical information is usually in logical or chronological sequence but rearrange it when culture requires: alter the sequencing and the proportion of given and new information within paragraphs (foregrounding, omitting, or repeating), because a structure that is logical for one language audience can be confusing for another.

Rearrange information within sentences, paragraphs, or chapters as needed — including to fix a poorly ordered source (for example, instructions that say to delete a file before backing it up) — but do not move entire chapters or sections without the client's permission, at minimum informing the client.

Apply Iconic Linkage: when the source expresses the same information several times with slightly different wording, pick one single translation and reuse it throughout, because doing so cuts the reader's cognitive effort, improves predictability and learning, looks consistent and professional, and makes translation memory more effective for pivot or relay translations.

In update projects, ethically and commercially tell the client that only a proportion of the text needs translating, accept translation-memory matches as is because they are already client-approved and changes ripple into relay translations, translate only the new sections while replicating the existing style and tone, and flag anything downright wrong to the client — preferably before changing it.

Establish whether the job is an instrumental translation (used in place of the source as a freestanding target text — so errors must be corrected) or a documentary translation (describing what the source said and how, as in back-translation or judicial use — so errors are preserved and shown, and back-translation is a limited quality check); in an instrumental translation the translator, as the expert, corrects simple linguistic errors, incorrect line breaks, text-versus-diagram mismatches, and obviously wrong units of measure (e.g. a 250 kg tablet where kg should be mg).

Expect source texts to contain errors (living texts are faulty texts), and decide whether to correct or preserve them by finding out from the client whether the job is instrumental or documentary; treat subject and factual errors as the trickiest category, since detecting them depends on your own subject knowledge and some standards (such as Germany's DIN 2345) place responsibility for source errors on the client.
Treat a publication-purpose translation as generally instrumental (so errors should be fixed), but do not assume an information-purpose text is documentary.
Recognize that not all of a technical document should be translated: some parts should not be translated at all, and others only in certain circumstances.

For quoted material from another publication, use an authoritative published target-language translation if one exists and can be obtained, rather than your own; if none is available, present a paraphrase that does not purport to be official — either omit the quote where the document permits, or give the source text with your paraphrase in square brackets marked as supplementary.
Keep a reference to a named law tied to the correct jurisdiction — a reference to a German law must remain about that German law, not another country's law that shares the name.

For EU texts between official languages, consult EUR-Lex for the authoritative translations of terminology and directive names; a directive carries a short reference code (year/identifier/abbreviation) plus a descriptive name, and because the abbreviation differs by language (EC, EG, ES, EY, EF, EK, KE, CE), select the correct short code for the target language and never leave the codes unchanged.

Recognize controlled languages (human-oriented for readability, machine-oriented for processing) and expect that a requirement to translate into a controlled language may force completely recasting sentences within its limited grammar and vocabulary, possibly enforced by a computerized style checker.

Comply with the client's style guide governing grammar, sentence structure, terminology, punctuation, address, headings, and product names: even a source-language style guide is useful, it may force you to change an initial choice (tense, direct speech, term), and typical rules include second-person address, present tense, positive constructions, consistent terminology, gerund rather than infinitive headings, no possessive product names, and no anthropomorphism.

Accommodate the client's mandated preferred terminology even when its rules (e.g. cancel but not abort, run but not execute) seem counterintuitive, because terminology problems are usually people-driven rather than about meaning; and require being notified of terminological and stylistic preferences and given the resources (style guides, glossaries) at the start, since a client cannot fairly complain about terminology they never supplied.

Treat readability tests (Flesch, Fog, Fry — each language-specific) as only a partial measure of quality: short, simple sentences raise readability, but a readable text is not necessarily good or effective, which is why usability now takes precedence over readability.

Optimize for usability — how well readers can read, understand, and perform or remember the task, and how unstressed they are afterward — by giving the right information in the right proportions at the right time and format, using these strategies: consistent terminology without polysemy, clear simple language, chronological instructions, direct and active language, no unnecessary information, Iconic Linkage, and a minimum of tenses.

Follow the golden rule: never return a translation without first running a spellchecker and reading through the text yourself, because a spellchecker finds misspelled words but not correctly spelled words that are the wrong words (it will not flag 'wit hall' for 'with all').

When revising another translator's work, find and fix errors rather than rewrite it as your own: verify that all information is accurate, terminology is correct and consistent, style suits the text and audience, and spelling, orthography, and punctuation are correct; provide a tracked-changes copy for the translator and a clean copy for the client; distance yourself for fresh eyes; stay objective and constructive; and never impose your own style — a change must be a genuine improvement, not a preference.

Never use footnotes in a professional translation to flag confusion or queries — because the translation may reach the end reader unreviewed, exposing your confusion and undermining credibility (annotated footnotes are only a student aid) — and instead keep a query record with page number and source sentence, send minor queries at delivery and serious ones by email while working, and reference them in the cover email so a busy project manager does not miss them.

Handle acronyms and abbreviations (used for brevity) by a chosen strategy: transfer (keep a well-known source acronym), reconstitute (build a new target acronym from the translated name, for non-specialized or ad-hoc cases), define (replace with a definition, useful for Latin abbreviations), combine (transfer plus definition once at first use), write out the source-language full name (for audiences who know the source culture), or translate (use an official translated name and its acronym).

Leave equations untouched (copy and paste) in most cases, while knowing that formulae can be rearranged to make another variable the subject and that equations may be embedded as images or inserted via special characters, ASCII codes, or an equation editor, so you can follow the text and reproduce any symbols in running sentences or in a hardcopy source.

Handle scientific symbols in running text carefully: copy and paste similar-looking symbols (such as R and the Greek rho, or the micro sign and the letter u) rather than retyping them, and change the font to disambiguate a character you cannot identify (for example a letter I versus the digit 1).

Leave units of measure unchanged wherever possible, especially SI quantities, because conversion is risky — the required rounding precision may be unknown, and in chemistry 1.06 mg differs significantly from 1.1 mg — and confusable prefixes and symbols (deci/deca, the micro sign versus u) invite error; leaving units alone ensures accuracy and prevents translator-induced error, especially for specialist audiences who know or can convert them.

In user-oriented texts prefer addressing the reader directly as 'you' over 'the user' because it is clearer and reduces misunderstanding, unless the audience strongly resists direct address; but a 'you'-favouring language does not license being overly familiar or using slang — it is still technical documentation.

Assume humour does not travel and gently remove jokes from technical texts (telling the client if unsure), and treat congratulatory content as potentially insincere or patronizing in some cultures; where humour must be kept because it serves a function (as in popular science), ensure it suits the audience and fulfils that function — by a non-humorous means if necessary.
Do not let the particular phrasing of a source term or description overly influence the translation, because different languages describe the same concepts from completely different angles.

On spotting an apparent error, notify the client and choose — by the text's length, subject, deadline, and the client's preference — whether to raise queries as you go or at delivery; handle errors by type: fix simple linguistic errors quietly, refer completely incomprehensible meaning to the client, fix minor factual errors but notify the client, and even for a serious error you are certain of, still contact the client for clarification.

Recognize and handle program code without being a programmer: commands and arguments resemble English words, but words written entirely in uppercase and multi-word tokens joined without spaces or by underscores (e.g. MENUITEM, Style_Caption) are usually non-translatable identifiers to leave unchanged, and in localization the translatable part is the on-screen strings.

In software menu strings, keep the ampersands that mark hotkeys (e.g. &View, F&ormat): do not delete them, mind their placement within the word, add no space immediately after them, and ensure the resulting hotkeys are unique.

Respect the syntax that runtime variables impose: where a string has two identical variables (e.g. 'Click %s to update %s'), preserve their order and rework the translation around it or the substitution will be wrong; and where a language lacks a consistent plural marker, replace plural variables with a rendering covering both forms (e.g. batch(es)), consulting the client or project manager when in doubt.
Do not translate commented-out code, which is not displayed in the finished product, except in rare cases such as sample files or training materials where you are explicitly asked to.

Apply the rules for translating around code: do not assume everything must be translated; do not translate underscore-joined or one-word compounds (CompanyName, File_Description); translate quoted text but leave quoted proper nouns (font, variable, or interface-element names such as 'scrollbar') untranslated; preserve trailing ellipses (Print...) and trailing spaces inside quotes used to concatenate strings; do not delete, modify, or rearrange variables; beware single-word strings like 'None' that may have gender-dependent translations; and ensure your translation matches the text that actually appears in the software.

Prefer numbered diagram labels; when word labels are embedded in the diagram as an image, supply the label translations in a three-column table rather than editing the image, since editing it requires a graphics editor and is not strictly the translator's job.

Never modify product or brand names even when they look funny, ungrammatical, or wrong, because they are proper names central to the product's identity and to its copyright protection (based on a specific spelling); transfer a specific brand named for a reason unmodified, and transcribe an internationally recognized brand exactly as in the source.

For a brand unknown in the target culture, do not blindly substitute a comparable target brand, since the two products may differ in characteristics or composition with consequences for repeatability or safety (e.g. in a chemistry paper); research first, then in specialist texts reproduce the brand name plus a brief function phrase, and in general texts use a comparable product qualified with 'such as' (to avoid implying endorsement) or a generic description.

Add Mr. or Ms. to a contact name when the target reader cannot tell the person's gender, and never translate email or website addresses (which breaks the address or sends readers to wrong-language content) — leave them and notify the client with suggested target-language alternatives.

Convert telephone numbers to international format with dialling codes and flag mobile numbers, and for postal addresses add the country or an international post-code prefix when the country is not identified, because the translation is read outside the source country.

Handle examples by type: replace culture-specific and context-based examples with scenarios familiar to the target audience, adapt language-specific examples heavily or invent new ones, and give technically-constrained examples only minimal modification unless there is language-specificity or different technical regulations apply.

When technical accuracy and linguistic fluency conflict, prioritize the technical, factual aspect over the linguistic; the balance depends on the text and subject, but the technical usually needs to take priority.

Translate warning and advisory information with particular care — it can be a matter of life or death and carries legal weight — and apply the notice severity hierarchy correctly (Note, then Warning for minor injury, Caution for equipment or data damage, Danger for serious or fatal injury), neither understating risk (so readers do not dismiss it) nor overstating it (using Danger where Warning fits dilutes the impact of Danger when truly needed).
Use the official EU-translated descriptions of standardized hazard symbols wherever the language combination permits, rather than translating them freshly.

Handle references to other documents by paraphrasing (when the precise name is unimportant), retaining (when the name matters but its meaning is clear), or retaining-and-paraphrasing (when the name matters but its meaning is not obvious — paraphrasing in the sentence or in square brackets in a list); for academic publications generally leave document names untranslated since they appear only in the bibliography, but transliterate author and publication names between different writing systems.

Expect scientific papers to arrive partially translated by well-meaning authors who speak the target language, and still take responsibility for handling and reconciling those pre-translated words, phrases, or paragraphs.

Handle Latin scientific and anatomical nomenclature (binomial genus-species names, stable and free of connotation) by retaining it (in italics, usually best for accuracy), explaining it (adding the common target-language name in parentheses for a lay or mixed audience, as in a patient information sheet), or replacing it (with the common name where the audience or language has no Latin exposure); find a Latin term's target meaning by searching it with a related target-language word, using a fuzzy or shorter-fragment search if it appears misspelled.
If a set of instructions does not make sense, contact the client to be walked through the process, and do not translate instructions you do not understand.

Test instructions by having someone follow them literally, using no common sense or problem-solving, which exposes weaknesses in how the information is explained, and calibrate the detail to the likely audience — neither so much that it patronizes nor so little that it confuses.

Do not translate an auto-generated table of contents first or in place: it is a projection of the actual heading text, so a translation typed into it is lost when the document is printed or updated — translate the real headings instead — and leave the table of contents until last, after the sections it describes, to avoid mistranslating headings out of context.

Be cautious about translating an auto-generated index first to use as a glossary, because translating terms out of context risks choosing the wrong term and forcing costly rework across the whole translation.

Meet strict space constraints (single-sheet leaflets, software string limits, diagram labels), knowing a translation naturally expands or contracts by language combination and direction, by using short simple words and sentences, clear abbreviations (preferably company or subject ones, without overuse), deviation from the source structure where a shorter target grammar allows, imperative verb forms, and flexible use of modulation, transposition, and adaptation.

Manage project files safely: create a project folder, keep a copy of the source files in a separate location with daily backups, overwrite the source with your translation using it as a template so formatting matches (never for PDFs, never by typing into a blank document), never work on the only copy (save under a new name first), and name translated files by keeping the original name plus the ISO target-language code.

Use the Internet as a terminology and subject resource: find parallel texts (restricting a search by the format a document type is typically published in) and use search operators — a tilde for synonyms, a minus for exclusion, and a source term plus a related target-language word to surface bilingual pages likely to contain a translation or glossary.

Assess online sources critically: rely on translator-forum answers only with extreme caution (there is no quality mechanism and answerers may lack your context), trust international, government, and state sites, use company sites for terminology (a localized one gives a bilingual resource), distrust supposedly impartial review sites and personal or free-hosted sites, and never rely on Wikipedia alone — corroborate anything found there.

Recognize addition (explicitation) as the procedure of adding information to a text during translation, motivated by the clarity of the target text, legal requirements, or political, cultural, and social factors.

Use House's covert/overt distinction — a covert translation is functionally equivalent and reads as though originally written in the target language, while an overt translation is evidently a translation whose source is tied to a specific time, culture, or language — and keep a text's purpose (its ultimate intended use) distinct from its function (its effect on the audience).

Treat a locale as all the linguistic, cultural, geographic, technical, and political factors that identify a target audience, and recognize a pivot (relay or indirect) translation as one routed through an intermediate language when no direct translator is available.

Always use the standardized international Hazard, Risk (R-phrases), and Safety (S-phrases) set phrases, with their authoritative official translations in the target language, when translating safety information — rather than translating the wording freely.

Treat ambiguous unit names with care: the 'ton' can be the metric tonne (1000 kg), the UK long ton (about 1020 kg), or the US short ton (about 907 kg), so identify which is meant before rendering or converting it.
